vignette:
Robert, a 61-year-old bus driver, came to treatment after months in which the nights had become the hardest part of the day. He described a long-ago torture experience that still entered his life in fragments: certain moments remained brutally vivid, while others were blank in a way that disturbed him almost as much as the memories themselves. When he tried to tell what happened, he could recall the sound of footsteps in a hallway, the feel of his own panic in his chest, and a few searing images with painful clarity, but the rest came in broken pieces, as though the story had been torn apart. Remembering it brought back the same terror he had felt at the time, and that terror made him feel cornered again, as if danger could return without warning even in his own home. Since then, he had become especially watchful after dark. He found himself listening for any sound that might mean someone was entering the house, pausing in bed to separate ordinary creaks from something more threatening, and it was hardest to settle when the neighborhood went quiet and his wife was asleep beside him.

As Robert spoke, it became clear that the way he understood the event had deepened the fear. He believed he had been weak in the face of what happened and said, with visible shame, that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop it. He also felt he should have protected others and failed them, a conviction that left him with the sense that he had not only survived something unbearable but had also fallen short of who he should have been. That judgment fed back into how he recalled the trauma: the clearer flashes seemed to him like evidence, proof of what he had endured and what he had not done, while the missing sections made him feel even more helpless, as if his mind had preserved the worst parts and abandoned the rest. The more he tried to piece it together, the more the incomplete picture became tied to self-blame, and each return of the memory seemed to confirm his belief that there was something fundamentally weak in him.

Over time, those beliefs sharpened his sense that danger was never far away. Robert began checking doors more than once before going to bed and keeping an ear open in the dark, especially on the nights when the memories were close. He said that after a disturbing recollection, his body would react strongly, and he would feel his heart kick up and his muscles brace as if the event were happening again. Those reactions made the night feel less safe than the day, and that feeling of vulnerability made his self-criticism even harsher. If he was so easily startled now, he reasoned, then perhaps he really was weak; if he could not feel safe in his own house, then perhaps he had failed to protect his family in some essential way. In that way, the fear of intrusion at night and the voice that called him inadequate had begun to feed each other, each confirmation making the other harder to shake.

The consequences had spread into his daily life as well. As a bus driver, Robert had to keep moving through streets, schedules, and ordinary conversations, but he carried a low-grade tension with him that made it harder to rest between shifts. Even at home, he was less present with his wife, not because he wanted distance but because he was constantly dividing his attention between the room he was in and the possibility of danger somewhere outside it. He finally sought help after a stretch of especially poor sleep, when he found himself awake late at night listening for sounds at the house and then spending the next day drained, ashamed, and preoccupied with the same old questions about why he had not done more. What brought him in was the fear that the nights would keep getting smaller and more dangerous in his mind, and what he most hoped for was relief from the terror, along with some way to believe he was not as weak or as culpable as he had come to think.
